title: Contra Gaudentium Donatistarum Episcopum
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa025.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: plane fideli apostolo, immo ipsi fideli deo, qui non sinit suos temptari supra quam ferre possunt, sed facit cum temptatione etiam exitum, ut possint sustinere, credant catholici, non credant Donatistae, et ne semper ista non credant, non sint Donatistae. quando enim desperatur in quibusque passionibus a domino impetranda patientia et ideo quaeritur compendium caminorum, ubi se isti non quidem feris, ut ait beatissimus Cyprianus, sed tamen flammis obiciunt, quos nemo damnauit, non est hoc consilium sed furor, non est sapientia sed amentia. habeant isti incendia sua, qui non dicunt de adiutorio domini: quoniam ab ipso patientia mea.
passages.english: Plainly, let Catholics believe the faithful apostle, or rather the faithful God himself, who does not allow his own to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation also makes a way out, so that they may be able to endure; let the Donatists not believe [him], and, so that they may not always disbelieve these things, let them cease to be Donatists. For when, in any sufferings whatever, people despair of obtaining patience from the Lord, and for that reason seek the short cut of the furnaces, where these men throw themselves, not indeed to wild beasts, as the most blessed Cyprian says, but still to flames, though no one has condemned them, this is not counsel but madness, not wisdom but insanity. Let these men keep their fires, who do not say of the Lord's help: "for from him is my patience."
passages.notes: "Compendium caminorum" is taken as "the short cut of the furnaces", that is, suicide by fire. The closing quotation is Psalm 61:6 (Vulgate numbering).

passages.original: ille namque contra te loquitur, qui uides quid dicat. per orbem totum dicit et per uniuersam terram porrigi extendique catholicam, Graeco eius nomini ac definitioni consentiens. tu aliud tenere sentire dicere reperiris et, dura Cypriano teste inniteris, Cypriano teste mentiris.
passages.english: For he speaks against you, and you see what he says. He says that the Catholic [Church] reaches out and extends through the whole world and through the entire earth, in agreement with its Greek name and definition. You are found to hold, think and say something else, and while you lean on Cyprian as witness, by Cyprian as witness you are shown to lie.
passages.notes: "dura" is probably a corruption of "dum" ("while"), and it has been translated as "while". "Ille" ("he") presumably refers to Cyprian.

passages.original: nam in ecclesia dicebatis manifesta zizania esse non posse, quotiens hoc testimonium Cypriani posuimus, et nec aperte illi resistere ausi estis nec tamen consentire uoluistis. nempe nunc saltem expergisceris audis aduertis, quia, etsi uidentur in ecclesia esse zizania, non tamen impediri debet aut fides aut caritas nostra, ut quoniam zizania esse in ecclesia cernimus ipsi de ecclesia recedamus. quare uos ergo ab unitate huius ecclesiae nefario schismate disceditis et haeretica praesumptione in eadem discissione persistitis? ecce tibi est Cyprianus: consenti illi aut responde illi. uides quemadmodum his uerbis, quibus dicit esse in ecclesia cernique zizania nec tamen ab illa propterea debere discedi, delet omnes tuorum scriptorum calumnias, quibus etiam in tanta abrupta progressus es et te more uestro praecipitasti, ut diceres etiam nescientes qui peccauerunt de uniuerso mundo peccatis alienis perire potuisse christianos, quia scilicet legitur in sanctis scripturis unum de anathemate fuisse furatum et pro isto peccato alienum populum nescientem fuisse punitum, ignorans illas mortalium corporum poenas, hoc est moriturorum mortes, ad utilem terrorem populo ualuisse, non tamen eisdem mortuis ad aliquod detrimentum futurae uitae aliena peccata, praesertim quae nescierunt, aliquid obfuisse.
passages.english: For you used to say that there could be no manifest tares in the Church, whenever we put forward this testimony of Cyprian, and you neither dared to resist him openly nor were willing to agree with him. Surely now at least you wake up, hear and notice that, even if tares are seen to be in the Church, neither our faith nor our charity ought to be hindered, so that we ourselves would withdraw from the Church because we see that there are tares in the Church. Why then do you depart from the unity of this Church by wicked schism, and persist in that same division with heretical presumption? Here is Cyprian for you: agree with him or answer him. You see how, by these words, in which he says that tares are in the Church and are seen there, and yet that one ought not on that account to depart from it, he wipes out all the slanders of your writings. In those writings you went forward into such steep places, and in your usual way threw yourself headlong, that you said that Christians throughout the whole world, even those who did not know who had sinned, could have perished through the sins of others. [You said this] because, of course, one reads in the holy Scriptures that one man stole from what was under the ban, and that for this sin a people who did not know of it were punished for another's [sin]. You did not know that those penalties on mortal bodies, that is, the deaths of people who were going to die anyway, served as a useful terror to the people, yet the sins of others, especially sins they did not know of, did no harm at all to those same dead with respect to any loss of the life to come.
passages.notes: "Alienum populum" is awkward. It has been taken as "a people [punished] for another's [sin]", and the text may be corrupt. The episode is Achan's theft of the devoted things in Joshua 7.
